---
title: "When it breaks"
subtitle: "Organised by what you saw, not by what is wrong"
---

Find the thing you saw in the left column. Most fixes are yours to apply; where one is your administrator's, the entry says so. Four entries carry more reasoning than a table cell holds and are written out below it.

Before anything else: if several things broke at once, or something that worked yesterday now fails at the connection, your token has probably expired. That surfaces as an opaque ODBC driver error rather than anything resembling an authentication message, so it gets debugged as a warehouse, driver or network fault. Sign in again first.

| What you saw | Why, and what to do |
|---|---|
| `No such file or directory` on a `/Volumes/...` path that definitely exists | That path is a filesystem path *inside* a cluster, and your own session cannot see it. Nothing is misconfigured and you have not mistyped it. Fetch the file first with `brickster::db_volume_read()`, then open it locally ([Read my files from a volume](../howdoi/volume-files.qmd)). |
| A shapefile read from a volume has lost its CRS | You fetched the parts rather than the directory, and the `.prj` was left behind. `st_read()` reports no error and `st_crs()` is `NA`, so nothing tells you until a measurement or a map comes out wrong. Use `db_volume_download_dir()` on the containing directory ([Read my files from a volume](../howdoi/volume-files.qmd)). |
| Polygons come back truncated or unreadable | Geometry is stored as `BINARY`, and the `odbc` path silently returns only part of a `BINARY` value. Read geometry over the `brickster` path instead, which [Connect your R session to the data](../howdoi/connect.qmd) sets up. This is not a preference between two working options: the `odbc` path cannot carry geometry (`r-dbi/odbc#1024`). |
| A `BINARY` value arrives far longer than it should be | A text representation of a geometry is being clipped at the default string column length. Set `DefaultStringColumnLength = 65535`; left at its default an encoded geometry is silently clipped at 1,023 characters. This bites a value a server-side spatial function produced, not only a column read from a table. |
| `unknown type 0` | An R object serialised into a `spark_apply()` body was encoded wrongly: either not `version = 2`, or the base64 has line breaks in it. Use `serialize(version = 2)`, then strip the line breaks. The message names neither cause, so check both. Better, if you have a volume: write the object to it and skip the whole mechanism ([Sending things to where your code runs](sending-things.qmd)). |
| A package upgrade appears not to have taken | It did take. Every R context gets its own library, and that library went away, so the version you are reading is the image's. Do everything that depends on an install inside one context, in one session, without a break. A durable fix needs a prebuilt library tree on a volume, and that is **your administrator's** ([Packages](packages.qmd)). |
| `install.packages("sf")` fails at configure | GDAL, GEOS and PROJ are absent from the runtime image. These are system libraries, not R packages, so no `install.packages()` argument changes it and you cannot do it from an R session. **Your administrator's:** forward [Setting up a cluster for geospatial R](../admin/geospatial-setup.qmd). |
| `terra` fails to load | Usually the same missing system libraries as above. On older runtimes there was a second cause: a `terra` pin against the image's GDAL, and an `Rcpp` upgrade before `units` would install. On DBR 18 neither pin is needed, so a script still carrying them is one to revise rather than a constraint to respect. **Your administrator's** ([Setting up a cluster for geospatial R](../admin/geospatial-setup.qmd)). |
| A spatial function is not recognised | Either the function does not exist on the compute you are connected to, or you have misspelled it. [See below](#a-spatial-function-is-not-recognised). |
| A distance, length or area is wildly wrong | Server-side measurement is planar, while `sf` on unprojected coordinates is spherical. [See below](#a-distance-length-or-area-is-wildly-wrong). |
| A spatial join or point-in-polygon count is off by a handful of rows | The same cause as the row above, in its quieter form. On longitude and latitude, `sf` and the server disagree about points sitting exactly on a boundary. [See below](#a-spatial-join-or-point-in-polygon-count-is-off-by-a-handful-of-rows). |
| `columns = list(...)` rejected | The documented list form of `spark_apply(columns =)` does not work here (`sparklyr/sparklyr#3529`). Use a Spark DDL string, `columns = "name type, name type"`, or omit the argument and let the types be inferred. Omitting works everywhere, which is the safest choice. |
| A `spark_apply()` column is missing, and the function looks fine | The right form of `columns =` depends on where you are running: a Spark type string from a client connection, a plain character vector on the cluster's own R session. Neither is rejected by the other path, and the error never mentions `columns`. Omit the argument, or match it to the context. This is why code moved between a notebook and a client session breaks ([Sending things to where your code runs](sending-things.qmd)). |
| `context =` rejected | `spark_apply(context =)` does not work on the `databricks_connect` backend, which is the backend a client connection uses. Use a volume to get the object across. The sparklyr documentation describing `context =` is not wrong, it just does not describe this backend. |
| Hashes differ between your session and a worker | The worker is probably on a different R patch release, and serialisation details differ between versions. Your object is fine. Compare content rather than hashes: row counts, a summary, `all.equal()` on the reconstructed object. |
| An R notebook refuses to attach to a cluster | Access mode: a Standard access mode cluster refuses R notebooks. [See below](#an-r-notebook-refuses-to-attach-to-a-cluster). |
| A `spark_apply()` job is slower than the serial version | Almost certainly nothing is wrong. Distributing costs serialisation, and if there is no second machine to distribute to, you pay the cost and get nothing back. [See below](#a-spark_apply-job-is-slower-than-the-serial-version). |
| `spark_apply(group_by = ...)` warns, then fails | The grouped path does not run on a current runtime, failing on `rpy2` 3.6.x with a warning from `pandas2ri.activate()` on the way. Use the partition-based form instead, without `group_by`. Do the grouping inside your function, or arrange the partitioning to match the groups you want. |
| An `sf` object written to a table comes back as text | `dbWriteTable()` on an `sf` object writes the geometry as a string column, silently, through the `brickster` backend. No error, and the table looks fine until you read it back. A table round trip is not lossless for spatial data: write geometry as well-known binary or text deliberately and convert on the way back, or keep the spatial object as a file on a volume ([Get results out, and get the same answer next year](../howdoi/results.qmd)). |
| A number that should be an integer is 0, or absurdly small | A Spark `BIGINT` arrives as `integer64`, and without `bit64` attached it converts to nonsense: 0, or something like `1e-320`. No warning. Use `library(bit64)`, or cast to a double in the query before collecting. |

## A spatial function is not recognised

The error is byte-identical whether the function is absent from your compute or you misspelled it, differing only in the name it quotes.

Check both, in that order, because the assumption most people make is backwards: an all-purpose cluster has *fewer* spatial functions than a warehouse, not more. Four are missing from the cluster, and `st_makepoint()` is the one you are most likely to hit. Use `st_point()` instead. [Which spatial functions you have](spatial-functions.qmd) has the list and the query that answers it for your own compute.

## A distance, length or area is wildly wrong

Your coordinates are longitude and latitude, and the measurement ran on the server. Nobody has made a mistake and nothing errors. The discrepancy can run to five orders of magnitude, because you are comparing metres with degrees.

`sf` treats longitude and latitude as points on a sphere and gives you metres. The server discards the coordinate system and does flat arithmetic in whatever units it finds, which for lon/lat means degrees. Both answers are correct to their own question.

Project your coordinates before you measure anything. That fixes it on both sides at once, because `sf` only reaches for spherical geometry when the data is unprojected: give it a projected CRS and it does flat arithmetic too, and the two agree. Doing the measurement in R is the other option, but it is the weaker one, because it only fixes the call you remembered to move.

Do not reach for `sf_use_s2(FALSE)`. It looks like the fix and is worse than the problem: see [Join and transform polygons](../howdoi/polygons.qmd#sf_use_s2false-and-st_setsrid-do-not-fix-it).

## A spatial join or point-in-polygon count is off by a handful of rows

The same cause as the entry above, and much harder to spot. If your data is in longitude and latitude and the predicate ran on the server, `sf` and the server disagree about points that sit exactly on a boundary, and they agree everywhere else.

A boundary is where a join puts its ambiguous records, so the rows that differ are precisely the interesting ones. Nothing is wrong by orders of magnitude, so nothing looks wrong at all: a count is a few rows out and both answers are defensible.

This is why "measurements are risky, true-or-false tests are safe" is not a rule you can rely on. Project first, and the disagreement goes away. [Join and transform polygons](../howdoi/polygons.qmd#sf_use_s2false-and-st_setsrid-do-not-fix-it) has the detail.

## An R notebook refuses to attach to a cluster

A client connection from your own R session to that same cluster works, which is what this guide assumes throughout, so you may not need the notebook at all.

If you specifically need notebook R, that is a cluster configuration change and belongs to your administrator.

## A `spark_apply()` job is slower than the serial version

On a single-node cluster `spark_apply()` was measured at roughly twice the time of forked parallel workers.

Check how many machines you have with [Work out what the cluster you have can do](../howdoi/compute.qmd). If `num_workers` is `0`, use the cores on the one machine you have rather than distributing. [Run a Monte Carlo simulation](../howdoi/monte-carlo.qmd) covers the choice.

## Next

If nothing above matches, the cause is often vocabulary rather than a fault: [Same thing, different words](words.qmd) translates the term in the error message. If it looks like a missing package, see [Packages](packages.qmd). If it looks like the shape of your compute, [Work out what the cluster you have can do](../howdoi/compute.qmd).
